content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain white bread is made from whole wheat where the bran and germ are retained. It has a soft white crumb, a light crust, and a mildly sweet flavor. This bread is suitable for everyday consumption and works well for sandwiches, toast, and as a side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain bread contains more fiber and nutrients than regular white bread.
Dough made with whole grain flour requires longer kneading and proofing times.
The white crumb is achieved by using the lighter part of the grain and a small amount of sugar.
In many countries whole grain bread is considered a staple of healthy eating.
When properly wrapped, the bread can stay fresh for up to 5 days at room temperature.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and B6 vitamins aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The bread provides magnesium, iron and zinc, essential for muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Lower glycemic index
items.content: Compared with refined white bread, whole grain varieties cause a slower rise in blood glucose.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Phytonutrients in whole grains help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease may experience severe reactions after eating the bread.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Gluten can be problematic for those following a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although healthier, the bread still provides calories, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties are salty; individuals with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread fresh, toasted, or as the base for sandwiches, wraps, soups and salads. It pairs well with avocado, low‑fat cheese, turkey, vegetables and nut butters.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bread in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature to keep the crust crisp. For longer storage, keep it in an airtight container in the refrigerator (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Thaw and warm before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Monster Zero Sugar is a zero‑calorie version of the popular Monster energy drink. It contains caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins and natural flavorings, but no sugar. Designed to boost alertness and concentration without raising blood glucose levels.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Monster Zero Sugar was launched in 2002 in response to growing demand for sugar‑free energy drinks.
It uses the artificial sweetener sucralose, which is about 600 times sweeter than sugar but contributes virtually no calories.
The drink provides 140 mg of caffeine per 12 oz (355 ml), comparable to a strong cup of coffee.
Each can contains taurine, an amino acid often linked to cardiovascular support.
Monster Zero Sugar is sold in more than 30 countries worldwide.

items.title: Increased energy and focus
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving alertness and reaction time.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: B‑vitamins (B2, B3, B6, B12) play key roles in energy metabolism, helping convert food into usable energy.

items.title: No sugar
items.content: The absence of sugar makes the drink suitable for people monitoring blood glucose levels.

items.title: Hydration contribution
items.content: While not a water substitute, the beverage adds fluid to the daily intake.

items.title: Excessive caffeine intake
items.content: High caffeine doses can cause anxiety, insomnia, rapid heartbeat, and increased blood pressure.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of certain stimulants and antidepressants.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Sucralose is safe in moderate amounts, but some individuals may experience gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Not recommended for children and pregnant women
items.content: Due to its high caffeine content, the product is not advised for children, adolescents, pregnant or nursing women.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Consume one 12‑oz (355 ml) can 30‑60 minutes before the activity that requires extra energy. Do not exceed 2‑3 cans per day. Avoid mixing with alcohol.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 7 days.

frozen-coffee-drink-with-whipped-cream.title: Frozen Coffee Drink with Whipped Cream

content.title: About
content.content: The frozen coffee drink with whipped cream is a refreshing dessert beverage made from cold espresso, milk, sugar, and a generous swirl of whipped cream. It is served as a thick, icy slush, often in a tall glass with a straw.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first frozen coffee drinks appeared in the United States in the early 1990s as a twist on traditional ice cream.
Whipped cream adds not only flavor but also the characteristic “fluffy” texture.
Variations may include flavorings such as vanilla, caramel, mint, or chocolate.
The drink is frequently topped with sprinkles, chocolate shavings, or caramel drizzle.
Although most popular in summer, many cafés serve it year‑round.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine enhances alertness and concentration.

items.title: Calcium from cream
items.content: Whipped cream provides calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Coffee is rich in B2 and B3 vitamins, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: The combination of sweetness and caffeine can lift mood.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: High caffeine intake may cause anxiety, insomnia, and rapid heartbeat.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Added sugar increases calories and may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Whipped cream contains lactose, which can cause discomfort for intolerant individuals.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to the cream.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the frozen coffee drink with whipped cream immediately after preparation to preserve its creamy texture. Feel free to add sprinkles, syrups, or fruit toppings to suit your taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. For best quality, consume within 1–2 weeks; longer storage may cause ice crystal formation.

content.title: About
content.content: Hot chocolate (cocoa) with whipped cream is a beverage made from cocoa powder, sugar, milk or water, topped with a light, airy whipped cream. It offers a rich chocolate flavor, sweet creamy notes, and the comforting aroma of a warm drink on a cold day.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cocoa powder is produced from fermented, dried, and roasted cacao beans.
The tradition of adding whipped cream to hot chocolate began in Europe in the 19th century.
In some countries hot chocolate is served with cinnamon, vanilla, or a pinch of sea salt.
Cocoa is rich in flavonoids, which give the drink its dark color and slight bitterness.
Whipped cream is made by beating fresh cream until soft peaks form, sometimes with added sugar or vanilla.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Cocoa stimulates the production of serotonin and endorphins, which can improve mood and reduce stress.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in cocoa is important for muscle and nerve function as well as energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cream
items.content: Whipped cream adds calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of sugars and the fats from cream provides a quick and sustained energy lift.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of tooth decay.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort from the milk and cream.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Whipped cream can trigger allergic reactions in individuals allergic to milk proteins.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Cocoa contains small amounts of caffeine and theobromine, which may affect sleep if consumed in large quantities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot chocolate with whipped cream in a mug, usually while hot. You can add a pinch of cinnamon, a dash of vanilla extract, or marshmallows. Apply the whipped cream just before serving to keep its airy texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cocoa powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. Keep cream refrigerated and use within a few days after whipping. Do not leave the prepared drink at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Soybeans (Glycine max) are legumes native to East Asia that have been cultivated for thousands of years. They are one of the world's most important crops and are eaten in many forms, from whole beans and edamame to tofu, tempeh, miso, natto, soy milk, and soy sauce. Soybeans are also used to make soybean oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Edamame are immature soybeans harvested while still green and eaten in the pod.
Soybeans are among the few plant foods that contain all essential amino acids.
Many traditional Asian foods are made from soybeans, including tofu, tempeh, miso, and natto.
Soybeans contain isoflavones, plant compounds that are being studied for their biological activity.
A large share of the world's soybeans is used for animal feed and oil.

items.title: Complete plant protein
items.content: Soybeans provide high-quality plant protein with all essential amino acids.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole soybeans provide fiber that supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Contains folate, iron, and vitamin K
items.content: These nutrients support cell function, oxygen transport, and blood clotting.

items.title: Provides magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals support muscle function and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Contains isoflavones and unsaturated fats
items.content: Soybeans contain isoflavones and mostly unsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy is one of the common food allergens, and people with soy allergy must avoid soy products and check labels.

items.title: Must be cooked
items.content: Raw soybeans contain compounds that interfere with digestion and should be properly soaked and cooked.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Soy can reduce the absorption of some thyroid medications. People taking these or having hormone-sensitive conditions should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Soybeans may cause gas or bloating in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whole soybeans can be soaked and boiled for soups, stews, and salads. Edamame can be steamed or boiled and eaten from the pod. Soy foods such as tofu, tempeh, miso, and soy milk are easy ways to include soy in meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried soybeans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked soybeans should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to five days or frozen. Edamame is often sold frozen. Tofu and other soy products should be stored according to their packaging.

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash (Cucurbita pepo) is the immature fruit of the zucchini plant, harvested while still tender. It is available in yellow or green varieties and can be eaten raw or cooked. When prepared, a small amount of fat (oil or butter) is often added to enhance flavor and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belongs to the cucurbit family, which also includes pumpkins, cucumbers, and melons.
Unlike many other squashes, it can be enjoyed raw, offering a crisp and mild taste.
The yellow hue comes from the natural pigment xanthophyll.
It is a staple in many world cuisines, from Italian ratatouille to Asian stir‑fries.
Fresh summer squash is very low in calories—about 17 kcal per 100 g.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Ideal for energy‑restricted diets and weight management.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect eye health and combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to cucurbit vegetables.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic squash, wash thoroughly to reduce residue exposure.

items.title: Excess fat during cooking
items.content: Using too much added oil increases the dish’s calorie density.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Summer squash can be sliced raw into salads, spiralized into “zoodles,” baked, sautéed, grilled, or steamed. When cooking, add 1‑2 tsp of oil to improve flavor and prevent sticking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store squash in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a perforated bag. It stays fresh for up to 5 days. Keep it away from ethylene‑producing fruits to slow ripening.

summer-squash-yellow-or-green-fresh-cook.title: Summer squash (yellow or green), fresh, cooked without added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash, also known as zucchini, are young fruits of the Cucurbitaceae family, typically yellow or green. When cooked without added fat they retain a delicate flavor, crisp texture, and very low calorie count, making them an excellent choice for healthy eating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belong to the same family as pumpkins, melons and cucumbers.
Unlike most squash, zucchini can be eaten raw, but cooking without fat preserves the most nutrients.
Yellow and green varieties differ only in skin color; taste differences are minimal.
They are a staple in low‑calorie dishes because they contain virtually no fat or carbs.
In Japan they are called “kakuri,” while in Italy they are known as “zucchini.”

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: 100 g of fresh summer squash provide about 17 kcal, ideal for weight management.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect eye health and combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cucurbit vegetables.

items.title: Pesticide residue
items.content: When buying non‑organic squash, wash thoroughly to reduce pesticide exposure.

items.title: Overconsumption
items.content: Large portions can cause gastrointestinal discomfort due to high fiber content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Summer squash can be steamed, baked, stewed, or quickly sautéed in a non‑stick pan without oil. Slice into rounds, half‑moons or cubes and add to salads, soups, stir‑fries, omelets, or grain bowls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store squash in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, loosely wrapped in a perforated bag. They stay fresh for up to 5 days. Keep them away from ethylene‑producing fruits.
